. The Honorable Rogers C. Morton U. S. Department of the Interior
Page 4
August 4, 1972
In the past year or so, many proposals have been made to not only restrict the use of public lands but to prohibit recreation vehicle use by classifying these areas as wilderness or primitive thereby denying use to some 98% of the national population. Since less than 2% of the nation's people are active hikers and backpackers, areas which restrict vehicle use become inaccessible to a very large majority. We have no quarrel with back-packing; however, the time required and the physical demands account for the relatively small number of people who are able to enjoy this type of activity. Surveys conclude that the majority of back-packers in the United States understandably are school teachers and students who have long summer vacations and are able to spend the long periods of time necessary to pursue this type of recreation. The average working man with two weeks annual vacation plus a few holiday weekends must restrict his recreational activities to those which may be reasonably pursued within a relatively short period of time.
It is interesting to note that the same groups who advocate increasing our country's wilderness areas and totally preserving our natural resources actively solicit and spend tax free funds to impair American commerce. These self-appointed guardians of the American public devote full time to lobbying and have filed lawsuits against nearly every large scale economically beneficial project which has been pursued by American industry during the past three to five years. Shocking examples of this unwarranted use of the country's judicial system are the halting of the Trans-Alaskan pipeline and the Florida Barge Canal. From where industry sits, it looks as if the government is "running scared" from a very vocal minority of the people.
Evidence of the preservationist impact on the United States economy is evidenced by the U. S. Chamber of Commerce's decision to take a stand against such groups, and to assume a more aggressive roll in shaping decisions being made not only by the courts, but by government agencies responsible for implementing environmental protection laws.
Areas which we feel worthy of exploration as a means of solving some of the problems created by the public's demand for outdoor recreation follow:
1. There are many tracts of government-owned land which at one time served as military reservations that are no longer in use which could be turned into recreation facilities to serve a portion of the close-in urban recreational needs.
2. The availability of low interest loans to recreational area development firms would stimulate development from the private sector.
